title: A hymn in Basant
hookLine: Ramanand sets out for the temple with sandalwood, and is turned back toward his own heart

lines: HE SETS OUT FOR THE TEMPLE.
cards: Sandalwood, ground into a paste on a stone. Fragrant oils in small bottles. A man gathers them up, the way you'd gather what you need for something important, and sets out to worship God in a temple.
He has everything ready. And somewhere between his door and the temple, his plan changes.
The man is the Bhagat Ramanand, and he tells the story himself, in a hymn the Gurus placed in the Basant section of the Guru Granth Sahib.

teach.b: The hymn begins at the end of the story, with a question. In paraphrase: where should I go?

teach.h: MY HOME IS COLORED WITH JOY.
teach.b: My own home has been colored with joy. My mind no longer wanders; it has gone still. Then he tells us how.
One day a longing rose in him. He ground sandalwood with fragrant oils and set out to worship God in the temple.

teach.h: SHOWN GOD IN HIS OWN HEART.
teach.b: But that God, he says, the Guru showed him inside his own heart. Wherever he went after that, he found the One already there, present in everything.
The hymn ends with thanks: he offers himself to the true Guru, who cut away his confusion and doubt, and names his Lord as the One who pervades all.

Tradition remembers Ramanand as a teacher other Bhagats looked to, and links Kabir with him; the hymn itself says nothing about that, so hold it as tradition. What the hymn does say is the turn from going to staying.
The sandalwood isn't mocked. The longing that sent him out the door is real, and the hymn honors it as the start of the story.
But the finding happens at home. And the word for what happens to his home is rang, the same word used for dye and for love. His house is dyed with it.
Yesterday the Granth spoke of a spring always present. Today Ramanand shows where it was all along: not out on the road, but in the house, in the heart.

how: Ramanand's hymn is sung in kirtan in Raga Basant, alongside the Gurus' own hymns; Sikhs honor the Bhagats whose words the Gurus placed in the Guru Granth Sahib.

games.q: what does “a hymn in basant” mean?
o: a spring song about planting sandalwood in the garden
Ramanand's hymn of finding God at home, in his own heart
Ramanand's hymn naming the best temple for spring worship

games.q: what's inside the hymn — tap the pairs.
p: gathered to worship in the temple
showed God in his own heart
a color word: dye, and love

s: Ramanand's hymn mocks the sandalwood and the trip
the longing that sent him out is the start of the story; the finding happens at home.
the hymn opens with a question: where should I go?
his home is already colored with joy, and his mind has gone still.

games.q: you're Ramanand. sandalwood ground, oils ready, you set out for the temple. what happens in the hymn?
o: you reach the temple and the story ends there.
the Guru shows you God inside your own heart.
you lose the sandalwood on the road.
games.why: the hymn says the Guru showed him the One in his own heart, and after that he found God present everywhere.

practice: If you can, play a shabad sung in Basant, or sit in the quiet, and notice the room around you exactly as it is: the light, the sounds, the slightly untidy corner, resisting the small urge to be somewhere better.

Then bring your attention to the breath and rest there, as if you've just come home after a long trip. If you pray, remember the One the hymn says is already present; if you don't, simply let this room be enough for now.

wordCard.voice: A hymn in Basant. Ramanand's song of setting out with sandalwood to worship, and being shown God in his own heart, so that his home is colored with joy. Today's word.

orig.note: rang: color, dye, and love; Ramanand's home is colored with it.

carryVoice: Your line: spring at home. Ramanand's longing set him on the road, and the finding happened at home. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Basant, Bani Bhagat Ramanand, 'Kat jaiai re ghar lago rang', Ang 1195
